name: Aesthetic Experience
statement: The distinctive, valued experience we have in appreciating art or the beauty of nature.
statementAccent: valued experience we have in appreciating art
meaning: Aesthetic experience is the distinctive kind of experience we have when we appreciate art or the beauty of nature, an experience many aestheticians have taken to be central to defining art, beauty, and the aesthetic. It is the valuable experience characteristically afforded by engaging with beautiful or artistically significant objects, and debates concern its nature, its features, and whether it can be defined at all. Two broad approaches divide the field. Internalist, or affect-oriented, theories define aesthetic experience by a special kind of felt experience, phenomenology, or absorption; externalist, or object-directed, theories define it by its being directed at features of an object, an experience of an object as having the aesthetic features it has. The concept emerged in eighteenth-century aesthetics, in Shaftesbury, Hutcheson, Hume, and above all Kant, whose Critique of the Power of Judgment of 1790 held that the judgment of taste rests on a disinterested pleasure, a pleasure without interest, not tied to desire or to the existence of the object, that is subjective yet claims universal validity and arises from the free play of imagination and understanding; disinterestedness became a central mark of the aesthetic. In the twentieth century, John Dewey's Art as Experience of 1934 treated aesthetic experience as a heightened, unified, consummatory experience, and Monroe Beardsley identified its features, such as focus, intensity, and unity, making it central to defining art. George Dickie's 1964 attack on the aesthetic attitude challenged the very idea of a special aesthetic state.
mechanism: Theories of aesthetic experience try to say what marks off the experiences we have in appreciating art and beauty from ordinary experience, and they locate the mark in different places. Internalist theories look inward, to the character of the experience itself: aesthetic experience is defined by a special phenomenology, a distinctive felt quality, pleasure, or state of absorbed attention, so that what makes an experience aesthetic is how it feels from the inside. Externalist theories look outward, to what the experience is about: aesthetic experience is an experience of an object as having the aesthetic features it has, its beauty, elegance, balance, or expressiveness, so that the aesthetic character of the experience derives from the aesthetic properties of its object. Kant's account supplied the tradition with several enduring ideas: that the pleasure taken in the beautiful is disinterested, indifferent to the object's usefulness or to whether it even exists, and that this pleasure, though grounded in feeling rather than concepts, lays claim to universal agreement and arises from a free, harmonious play between the imagination and the understanding. Later theorists developed the notion in different directions. Dewey emphasized the way an aesthetic experience gathers ordinary experience into a complete, unified, and fulfilling whole, an experience that reaches consummation. Beardsley enumerated phenomenological features, focus, intensity, and unity, and tied them to a functional definition of art as intended to afford such experience. Against all this, Dickie argued that there is no distinctive psychological state or mode of attention at all, only ordinary attention differently directed, so that the very notion of a special aesthetic experience or attitude may be a myth.

examples.text: Kant held aesthetic pleasure is disinterested, indifferent to desire or the object's existence, yet claims universal validity.
Dewey treated aesthetic experience as a heightened, unified, consummatory experience that completes and fulfills.
Dickie argued there is no special aesthetic state, only ordinary attention differently directed, calling it a myth.

variants.name: Internalist versus externalist
variants.text: Defining aesthetic experience by its felt phenomenology, or by its being directed at an object's aesthetic features.

variants.name: Disinterestedness
variants.text: Kant's mark of the aesthetic, a pleasure taken without interest in desire or the object's existence.

whyItMatters: Aesthetic experience is one of the organizing concepts of the philosophy of art and the theory of the aesthetic, and much in aesthetics has been built on it. Many of the field's central questions, what art is, what beauty is, what aesthetic value consists in, have been answered by appeal to a distinctive kind of experience that art and beautiful things afford, so that clarifying aesthetic experience promises to clarify the aesthetic domain as a whole. The concept carries the legacy of the eighteenth-century invention of aesthetics and of Kant's enormously influential analysis of disinterested pleasure, which shaped the whole tradition of thinking about the aesthetic and gave rise to the aesthetic-attitude theories that define the aesthetic through the subject's mode of attention. It underwrites functional definitions of art, such as Beardsley's, on which art is understood as made to produce aesthetic experience. And it is the focus of a deep skeptical challenge, from Dickie and others, over whether there really is any distinctive aesthetic state or natural kind, or only ordinary experience aesthetically described. As the valued experience at the heart of our engagement with art and beauty, aesthetic experience is a foundational and much-debated topic in aesthetics.

working.text: engage with a work of art or a beautiful natural scene in appreciation.
identify what makes the experience aesthetic, whether its felt quality or its direction at an object's aesthetic features.
ask whether there is a distinctive aesthetic state at all, or only ordinary attention differently directed.

limits: The notion of aesthetic experience is central but contested, and even its existence as a distinctive kind has been challenged. The internalist and externalist approaches pull in different directions, and it is disputed whether the aesthetic character of an experience is best located in its phenomenology or in its object, with each facing counterexamples. The most pointed challenge is skeptical: George Dickie, in The Myth of the Aesthetic Attitude of 1964, argued that there is no special mode of disinterested attention or distinctive psychological state, only attention that is more or less close and variously directed, so the supposed aesthetic experience may be a philosopher's construction rather than a genuine natural kind. Defining aesthetic experience precisely enough to do the theoretical work asked of it, grounding the definition of art or of aesthetic value, has proven difficult, and characterizations by focus, intensity, and unity are debated. Some historical attributions and datings reward care: Kant's Critique dates to 1790, Dewey's Art as Experience to 1934, and Dickie's essay to 1964, and standard characterizations should be treated as summaries rather than exact quotations. So aesthetic experience robustly names the valued experience of appreciating art and beauty, understood as a central concept whose nature, and even whose distinctness, remain disputed.
misreadings: Aesthetic experience is not simply any pleasant experience; on the Kantian tradition it is marked by disinterestedness, a pleasure indifferent to desire and to the object's usefulness. It is not obviously located solely in the subject, since externalist theories tie it to the aesthetic features of the object. And it is not an uncontested given, since Dickie and others question whether any distinctive aesthetic state exists, so treating aesthetic experience as mere pleasure, as purely subjective, or as beyond doubt, misreads the concept.
origin: The distinctive, valued experience of appreciating art or natural beauty, central to defining art and the aesthetic, developed from eighteenth-century aesthetics and Kant's disinterested pleasure through Dewey and Beardsley and challenged by Dickie.
